title: Campania
description: Volcanic hills around Naples: Taurasi, Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo.
L: Explain the role of volcanic soils

Campania, in southern Italy, runs from the coast around Naples and the Amalfi coast inland to the hills of Irpinia. Its key wine areas are inland, around Avellino, at 300 to 700 m. Mount Vesuvius and the Campi Flegrei near Naples are volcanic; Irpinia has volcanic ash over clay and limestone.

Volcanic soils drain well and are rich in minerals; in sandy volcanic areas phylloxera struggled, so some ungrafted vines survive. Inland Irpinia, despite being in the south, has a cool, almost continental climate with snow in winter and late harvests, sometimes in November. That keeps acidity high.
Why does Irpinia make fresh wines in southern Italy?
Altitude gives a cool, almost continental climate
Height and inland position cool it down.

Campania was a centre of Roman wine. Falernian, from northern Campania, was the most famous wine of ancient Rome. The Greeks brought vines here; Greco's name suggests that heritage. Pompeii, destroyed by Vesuvius in 79 AD, was a wine-trading town, and vines have been replanted inside its ruins.
Falernian, from Campania, was ancient Rome's most famous wine.
Yes. It was praised by Roman writers.
Campania's best wines come from Irpinia's hills
Volcanic soils and altitude give freshness
It was a centre of Roman wine

Aglianico is Campania's great red: dark, with high tannin and high acidity, black cherry, smoke and earth. It ripens very late. It makes Taurasi DOCG, often called the Barolo of the south, which must be at least 85% Aglianico and age three years, one in wood; Riserva four years. Mastroberardino kept the tradition alive after the Second World War.

Fiano di Avellino DOCG gives textured, nutty whites with pear, hazelnut, honey and smoke, that can age 10 years or more. Greco di Tufo DOCG, from sulphur-rich volcanic soils around Tufo, gives firmer, mineral whites with peach and almond. Falanghina, near Naples and Benevento, gives fresh, floral whites; Piedirosso a light red.
Match each wine to its grape.
Campania's three DOCGs are all in Irpinia.
Fiano di Avellino gains honey and smoky notes with age. A five-year-old bottle is often better than a young one.
Which DOCG is often called the Barolo of the south?
For Aglianico's tannin, acidity and ageing potential.
Aglianico makes Taurasi, structured and long-lived
Fiano is nutty; Greco is mineral
Falanghina and Piedirosso complete Campania's grapes
Reading Campania and eating with it

Campania's three DOCGs, Taurasi, Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo, are all in Irpinia. Other names include Irpinia DOC, Falanghina del Sannio, Campi Flegrei, Lacryma Christi del Vesuvio, from Vesuvius' slopes, and Costa d'Amalfi. Riserva on Taurasi means at least four years of ageing.

Campania's food suits its wines: Fiano with buffalo mozzarella and seafood; Greco with fried fish and pasta with clams; Falanghina with pizza margherita; Taurasi with Neapolitan ragù, slow-cooked meat sauce, lamb and aged cheese. Serve whites at 10 to 12, Taurasi at 16 to 18, decanted.
Mozzarella with Fiano, ragù with Taurasi
Slow-cooked meat sauce suits Aglianico's tannin.
Lacryma Christi, the tears of Christ, is a legendary name for wine from Vesuvius' slopes, red from Piedirosso and white from Coda di Volpe.
